# Cunda Sutta (Snp 1.5 (PTS Snp 16))

**ID:** Snp 1.5 (PTS Snp 16)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Cunda Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

These four classes comprise the path-conqueror (*maggajina*), the path-teacher (*maggadesaka*), the path-liver (*maggajīvin*), and the path-corrupter (*maggadūsin*); S. M. Katre points out that this scheme reflects degrees of spiritual attainment rather than sectarian affiliation [Katre 1931]. G. C. Pande notes that although the discourse is entirely centered on the concept of the path (*maggo*), it makes no mention of the eightfold division of the path [Pande 1974]. Metrically, K. R. Norman observes that verses 83–90 are composed in the Aupacchandasaka metre, except for verse 88a, which is Vaitālīya [Norman 1997-2001].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Passage-level parallels: DA 2 遊行; T 5 佛般泥洹; T 6 般泥洹; sf245 Mahāparinirvāṇa
- Resembling parallels: T 7 大般涅槃

**Sources**

- [Katre 1931] S. M. Katre, Early Buddhist Ballads and Their Relation to Older Upanishadic Literature (1931) — Discussed the four classes of samaṇas in Sn 83–90 as indicators of attainment.
- [Norman 1997-2001] K. R. Norman, The Group of Discourses (Sutta Nipāta) (1997–2001) — Identified the metrical forms of the sutta as Aupacchandasaka and Vaitālīya.
- [Pande 1974] Govind Chandra Pande, Studies in the Origins of Buddhism (1974) — Observed that the discourse discusses the path without referencing the eightfold path.
